text: The following is a list of notable non-arterial streets in Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Bremner Boulevard

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Bremner Boulevard is a short street in downtown Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street is notable for having several landmarks are located on the street , including the Rogers Centre , the CN Tower , the Toronto Railway Museum , Ripley 's Aquarium of Canada , the Delta Toronto Hotel , Maple Leaf Square , and the west entrance to Scotiabank Arena .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Following the Toronto Raptors victory in the 2019 NBA Finals , the section of Bremner Boulevard from York Street to Lake Shore Boulevard West was renamed Raptors Way .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Bond Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Bond Street is a short street from Gould Street to Queen Street East , it is home to many historic buildings and associations with many historical figures of the city .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Colborne Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Colborne Street is a street running several hundred metres east of Yonge Street in downtown Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It crosses Victoria Street and Leader Lane , ending at Church Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It is located between and parallel to King Street East and Wellington Street East .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street is notable for retaining several historic buildings built during the reign of Queen Victoria .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: De Grassi Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: De Grassi Street is a side street located in Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It was named after Captain Filippo " Philip " De Grassi , an Italian - born soldier who immigrated to Canada with his family in 1831 and settled in York , Upper Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It is best known in popular culture as the namesake of the teen drama television franchise Degrassi , with the first three series shot in and around the street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Draper Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Draper Street is a street in downtown Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It is a north – south street located to the west of Spadina Avenue , from Front Street West north to Wellington Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Draper Street is notable for its collection of twenty - eight 19th Century Second Empire - styled row cottages .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The houses were designated by the City of Toronto in the 1990s to have heritage status .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The entire street is designated as a Heritage Conservation District as a way to preserve its heritage for posterity .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street is named after William Henry Draper , a lawyer , judge , and politician in Upper Canada later Canada West .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street was laid out in an 1856 plan of subdivision by J. Stoughton Dennis of lands that were part of the 1794 Garrison Reserve .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Draper and Charles Jones are listed as the property owners of the lots to be subdivided for development .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street is narrow ; it is only 32 feet ( 9.8 m ) - wide .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The lots are all 88 feet ( 27 m ) deep and vary in width from 22 feet ( 6.7 m ) to 32 feet ( 9.8 m ) wide .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The Esplanade

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The Esplanade is an east – west street along the central waterfront of Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Originally conceived as a city beautification project to clean up the city 's waterfront in the 1850s , the street was taken over by the coming of the railways to Toronto in 1850 .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The railway eventually moved to an elevated viaduct , leaving only the eastern section of the street today .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The area , east of Yonge Street , was dominated by industrial uses until the second half of the 20th Century .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: As the harbour declined as a transfer point , the railway and industrial uses left the area .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The Esplanade was redeveloped into a residential area , known as the " St. Lawrence Neighbourhood " in the late 1970s and early 1980s .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: This neighbourhood consists of generally low - rise and mid-rise housing - condominiums , public housing , cooperatives and some town homes between Jarvis and Parliament Street south of Front Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: In the blocks between Jarvis and Parliament the southern part of the street ( and the former rail tracks ) - were converted to a long strip of park and recreation space for the residents - David Crombie Park .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The stretch between Scott Street and Market Street is a popular restaurant area .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: George Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: George Street is a north – south street in Toronto , Ontario , Canada , from south of Front Street , north to Gerrard Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It s southern blocks are within the grid of the townsite of the original town of York , Upper Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: George Street was once one of the most exclusive and expensive addresses in the city .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Today , the north end of the street , next to Seaton House men 's shelter , is an example of urban blight .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Graffiti Alley

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Graffiti Alley , officially Rush Lane , is a three - block alleyway in Toronto 's Fashion District , known for hosting street art .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Lonely Planet has called the site " possibly the most popular place to check out street art in Toronto " .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Despite its popularity with tourists and leniency by law enforcement , it is not a legal wall .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: John Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: John Street is one of several in the area named after the first Lieutenant Governor of Upper Canada and founder of York , Upper Canada , John Graves Simcoe .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street begins on Front just north of Metro Toronto Convention Centre and north to Stephanie Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: North of Stephanie , the street becomes a pedestrian walkway towards Grange Park and the Art Gallery of Ontario .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: South of Front , John becomes a pedestrian walkway between the Rogers Centre and the CN Tower .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Leader Lane

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Leader Lane is a short street in Toronto , Ontario , Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street was part of the former city of York , Upper Canada .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It runs from Wellington Street to King Street , crossing Colborne Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street was renamed Leader 's Lane after the Toronto Leader , a newspaper whose offices were located there from 1852 to 1878 .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It was the site of York 's first jail and " hanging yard " .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Markham Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Markham Street is a north – south residential street located in the city of Toronto , Ontario , Canada , one block west of Bathurst Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It s northern end starts in the Seaton Village neighbourhood and it passes through Mirvish Village , Palmerston – Little Italy , Trinity – Bellwoods and ends at West Queen Street West at its south end .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Palmerston Boulevard

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Palmerston Boulevard is a residential street located in the city of Toronto , Ontario , Canada , two blocks west of Bathurst Street , between Koreatown and Little Italy .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street is bounded by stone and iron gates both at Bloor Street and College Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Notably , it is lit with symmetrically placed cast-iron lamps and canopied by mature silver maple trees .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Raymore Drive

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Raymore Drive is a mostly residential street in the Weston neighbourhood of Toronto in the Canadian province of Ontario .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It runs next to the Humber River .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: On October 15 , 1954 , the area was severely affected by Hurricane Hazel .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: When the Humber River burst its banks and tore away a footbridge , the waters of the Humber were redirected through the neighbourhood .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The flood killed 35 residents and washed away 39 percent of the street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The washed - away part of Raymore Drive was never rebuilt , as subsequent residential development in that area has been prohibited ; it is now part of Raymore Park .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Rees Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Rees Street is named for Dr William Rees ( 1800 – 1874 ) , a physician who provided health services to immigrants to the city in the 19th Century , as well as being an advocate for social reform and public services .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Rees established at public bath on wharf , which was informally named Rees Wharf at the foot of Peter / John Street ( now lies somewhere between Rogers Centre and the CN Tower ) .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: After Rees ' death , the wharf became the Water Works , a water pumping station .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Reggae Lane

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Reggae Lane is a roadway that runs east from Oakwood Avenue , behind a strip of buildings on the south side of Eglinton Avenue in the Eglinton West ethnic enclave also known as Little Jamaica .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: For most of its history , it had no official name , but the imminent arrival of Oakwood LRT station of Line 5 Eglinton helped trigger its 2015 official naming by Josh Colle .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The neighbourhood near Reggae Lane was recognized as a centre for reggae recording as early as the late 1960s .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Simcoe Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Simcoe Street is a street in Toronto named for first Lieutenant Governor of Upper Canada ( now Ontario ) John Graves Simcoe .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: From Queen 's Quay to Front Street West it is called Lower Simcoe Street connecting via the Simcoe Street Tunnel beneath tracks west of Union Station ( Toronto ) .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: This section was result of infilling of harbour south of Front Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: From Wellington Street West north to Queen Street West , Simcoe Street is a southbound only for cars with a contraflow bike lane .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: North of Queen Street , it continues briefly as a pedestrian only street to Michael Sweet Avenue behind Canada Life Building , Ontario Superior Court of Justice and close to US Consulate .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Prior to mid 1850s it was called Graves Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The section north of Queen Street was previously called William Street until 1870s .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: York Street

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: York Street is one of the oldest streets in Toronto .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: It extends from Toronto Harbour north to Queen Street one block west of Bay Street .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: At Front Street , University Avenue merges into York Street south of Front .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: To the east at Front Street is Union Station and the Royal York Hotel .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: At its northern end is Osgoode Hall and the Sheraton Centre hotel .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: In the early years of Toronto , York Street was the ' red - light district ' of Toronto .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The stretch between King and Queen streets contained ten known brothels , several assignation houses , eight unlicensed bars that served " maddening liquor to the depraved masses " , and second - hand dealers who would move stolen goods and hide illegal stashes of whisky .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: Constables would start investigations of crimes by visiting York Street , expecting criminals to be found there , as in a case in 1883 when two women who stole a drunken farmer 's watch were arrested in a York Street bar shortly afterwards .

source.page_title: List of notable streets in Toronto

text: The street was embarrassing to Toronto citizens who worried about " the opinion of strangers who are dumped from the train into one of the most disreputable streets that every existed in any city . "

text: In the 1950s and 1960s , a " third vinyl format " was introduced alongside long - playing ( LP ) albums , and singles .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The extended play ( EP ) used the same formats as singles but contained more tracks .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: Singles were the popular record format at the time – predominantly 10 - inch 78 rpm and 7 - inch 45 rpm formats – and the first singles chart was published by the New Musical Express in 1952 , with many other publications also producing singles charts in the 1950s and 1960s .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: Record Mirror published the first album chart in 1956 , and when Record Retailer began compiling an LP chart on 12 March 1960 , they also compiled an EP chart .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The EP chart consisted of a top ten , and was expanded to fifteen positions the following week , and twenty the week after that .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: EPs " died out in the late 1960s " , and Record Retailer reduced the chart to ten positions on 16 April 1966 , publishing the final EP chart on 16 December 1967 .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: For six weeks in 1966 and two weeks in December 1967 , Record Retailer did not publish EP charts , but they were compiled , and Record Mirror published them ; Record Mirror had begun publishing charts compiled by Record Retailer in March 1962 , following a decision to stop compiling their own albums and singles charts .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The longest consecutive duration at the top of the chart was 23 weeks for The Shadows ' EP The Shadows to the Fore .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The most weeks at number one was achieved by The Beach Boys ' EP Hits , which spent 34 weeks there from June 1966 , and was the incumbent number one when the chart ceased at the end of 1967 .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The Beatles had eight different EPs top the chart , as did The Shadows ( four with Cliff Richard and four on their own ) .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: The Shadows spent 69 weeks with an EP on top of the chart in comparison to The Beatles ' 63 weeks .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: Conversely , only four acts spent a total of one week atop the chart ; Joan Baez , Jim Reeves , the George Mitchell Minstrels and Bobby Vee ( with The Crickets ) .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: Although official music recording sales certifications were not introduced until the British Phonographic Industry was formed in 1973 , Disc introduced an initiative in 1959 to present a silver disc to records selling over 250,000 units .

source.page_title: List of number-one EPs in the United Kingdom

text: Seven EPs are recorded as going silver : The Beatles ' number - one EPs Twist and Shout , The Beatles ' Hits , All My Loving , Long Tall Sally , as well as The Beatles ( No . 1 ) and Magical Mystery Tour ( which did not reach number one but would have done so had the EP chart lasted only a few more weeks ) and The Rolling Stones ' number - one EP Five by Five .

text: A logging camp ( or lumber camp ) is a transitory work site used in the logging industry .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Before the second half of the 20th century , these camps were the primary place where lumberjacks would live and work to fell trees in a particular area .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Many place names ( e.g. Bockman Lumber Camp , Whitestone Logging Camp , Camp Douglas ) are legacies of old logging camps .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Camps were often placed next to river tributaries so that the winter 's log harvest could be floated to the lumbermills in the spring .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: The requirements of the logging industry involved the creation of a working site and housing from the pristine wilderness .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: The construction of the logging camp consisted of a transformation of the natural environment to the built environment .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Logging was seasonal in nature , with farmers often working as lumberjacks during the winter .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Camps were placed next to a river so that the logs harvested could be floated to the lumbermills in the spring .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: By their nature logging camps were temporary work sites used to harvest lumber in remote areas .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Once the lumber in a particular area was harvested , the lumberjacks would move on .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Primitive sites had two buildings , a cookhouse and a bunkhouse .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Larger camps also had an outhouse , barn , blacksmith shop , filer shack ( to sharpen the saws ) , office and camp store .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Lumber cut by the lumberjacks was the source of the materials for the buildings , and camps were built in the fall prior to the winter logging season .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Most of the lumberjacks would return to their jobs after the logging season , with a few staying on to drive logs in the spring .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: In the United States , logging camps were phased out after World War II , as work crews could more easily be transported to remote logging sites .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Camp food

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Lumberjacks could work upwards of twelve hours a day , and lumbering was such physically demanding work that each man could eat between 6,000 and 9,000 calories a day .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: In one estimation , the average logger consumed 5 pounds ( 2.3 kg ) of food each day .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Quality and quantity were important parts of maintaining the health and productivity of the workers .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Meat , other foods high in protein , and fats were served in abundance .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Sack lunches were provided to the loggers .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: During peak season , as many as five meals a day could be served .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: Camp cooks were important to the morale of the workers .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: In some cases , workers would follow a cook to the camp they were working at each season .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: In Canada , the long distances to the camps and the closure of most access during the winter led to the development of depot farms that would be built near logging camps to supply cereals and vegetables to the loggers as well as food for horses in the form of hay and oats .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: These farms were often built on poor quality land and had little output other than the camps and self - consumption , and most often closed as soon as the camp did .

source.page_title: Logging camp

text: See also Holt and Balcom Logging Camp No. 1 Camp 6 Logging Museum Man camp

text: The London , Brighton and South Coast Railway ( LB&SCR ( known also as the Brighton line , the Brighton Railway or the Brighton ) ) was a railway company in the United Kingdom from 1846 to 1922 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It s territory formed a rough triangle , with London at its apex , practically the whole coastline of Sussex as its base , covering a large part of Surrey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was bounded on its western side by the London and South Western Railway ( L&SWR ) , which provided an alternative route to Portsmouth .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On its eastern side the LB&SCR was bounded by the South Eastern Railway ( SER ) — later one component of the South Eastern and Chatham Railway ( SE&CR ) — which provided an alternative route to Bexhill , St Leonards - on - Sea , and Hastings .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR had the most direct routes from London to the south coast seaside resorts of Brighton , Eastbourne , Worthing , Littlehampton and Bognor Regis , and to the ports of Newhaven and Shoreham - by - Sea .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It served the inland towns and cities of Chichester , Horsham , East Grinstead and Lewes , and jointly served Croydon , Tunbridge Wells ( preserved as the Spa Valley Railway ) , Dorking and Guildford .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At the London end was a complicated suburban and outer - suburban network of lines emanating from London Bridge and Victoria , and shared interests in two cross-London lines .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was formed by a merger of five companies in 1846 , and merged with the L&SWR , the SE&CR and several minor railway companies in southern England under the Railways Act 1921 to form the Southern Railway from 1 January 1923 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Origins of the company

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The London , Brighton and South Coast Railway ( LB&SCR ) was formed by an act of Parliament , the London and Brighton Railway Act 1846 ( 9 & 10 Vict. c. cclxxxii ) , on 27 July , through the amalgamation of a number of railway companies :

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The London and Croydon Railway ( L&CR ) , created in 1836 and opened in 1839 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The London and Brighton Railway ( L&BR ) , created in 1837 and opened in 1841 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Brighton and Chichester Railway , created in 1844 and opened in stages between November 1845 and June 1846 , with an extension to Havant under construction at the time of amalgamation .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Brighton , Lewes and Hastings Railway , created in February 1844 , opened in June 1846 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Croydon and Epsom Railway , created in July 1844 , under construction at the time of amalgamation .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Only the first two were independent operating railways : the Brighton and Chichester and the Brighton , Lewes and Hastings had been purchased by the L&BR in 1845 , and the Croydon and Epsom was largely owned by the L&CR . )

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The amalgamation was brought about , against the wishes of the boards of directors of the companies , by shareholders in the L&CR and L&BR who were dissatisfied with the early returns from their investments .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR existed for 76 years until 31 December 1922 , when it was wound up as a result of the Railways Act 1921 and merged with the London and South Western Railway and the South Eastern and Chatham Railway to form the Southern Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Original routes ( Dates of opening from F. Burtt The Locomotives of the London Brighton and South Coast Railway 1839 – 1903 . )

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At the time of its creation the LB&SCR had around 170 route miles ( 274 km ) in existence or under construction , consisting of three main routes and a number of branches .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main line to Brighton from London Bridge opened in 1841 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The sections between Corbett 's Lane ( New Cross ) and London Bridge and between Croydon and Redhill were shared with the South Eastern Railway ( SER ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were two branch lines under construction at the time of the amalgamation : the Sutton & Mole Valley Lines from Croydon to Epsom ( opened 10 May 1847 ) , and the Arun Valley Line from Three Bridges to Horsham ( opened 14 February 1848 ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The West Sussex coast line originated with a branch line from Brighton to Shoreham , opened 12 May 1840 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This had been extended to Chichester by the time of the amalgamation , and a further extension to Havant was under construction ( opened 15 March 1847 ) , with the ultimate aim of extending the line to Portsmouth .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The East Sussex coast line from Brighton to Lewes and St Leonards - on - Sea , with running powers over the SER to Hastings , opened 27 June 1846 , one month before the amalgamation , with branches to Newhaven ( opened 8 December 1847 ) , Eastbourne and Hailsham ( opened 14 May 1849 ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A connecting spur from the Brighton main line at Keymer Junction near Haywards Heath to the Brighton – Lewes line was under construction at the time of amalgamation , opening in October 1847 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A short line from New Cross to Deptford Wharf , proposed by the L&CR , was approved in July 1846 , shortly before amalgamation , but was not opened until 2 July 1849 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The use of this line for passengers would have contravened the recently negotiated agreement with the SER that the LB&SCR would not operate lines to the east of its main line , and it was restricted to goods .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A short branch from this line to the nearby Surrey Commercial Docks in Rotherhithe opened in July 1855 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: London stations

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main London terminus was the L&CR station at London Bridge , built by the London and Greenwich Railway ( L&GR ) in 1836 , and exchanged for the original L&CR station in 1842 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: For the first few years of its existence , LB&SCR trains used the L&GR lines from Corbett 's Lane into London , but by 1849 the viaducts had been widened sufficiently for its own tracks .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR inherited from the L&CR running powers to the smaller SER passenger terminus at Bricklayers Arms .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Poorly sited for passengers , it closed in 1852 and was converted into a goods station .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR owned three stations at Croydon , later East Croydon ( former L&BR ) Central Croydon and West Croydon ( former L&CR ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Atmospheric lines

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The L&CR had been partially operated by the atmospheric principle between Croydon and Forest Hill , as the first phase of a scheme to use this mode of operation between London and Epsom .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , following a number of technical problems , the LB&SCR abandoned atmospheric operation in May 1847 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This enabled it to build its own lines into London Bridge , and have its own independent station there , by 1849 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The history of the LB&SCR can be studied in five distinct periods .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Relations with neighbouring railways , and the beginnings of expansion 1846 – 1859

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was formed at the same time as the bursting of the railway mania investment bubble , and so it found raising capital for expansion extremely difficult during the first years of its operation , other than to complete those projects that were already in hand .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The L&BR had experienced difficult relations with the SER where the companies shared facilities , notably at Redhill and Hastings and on the approaches to London Bridge .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In October 1849 the SER acquired the new Reading , Guildford and Reigate Railway ( RG&RR ) line , which the LB&SCR regarded as a major incursion into its territory .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , the LB&SCR had one important playing card not available to the L&BR — control of the SER main line between New Cross and Croydon .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1849 the LB&SCR appointed a new and capable chairman , Samuel Laing , who negotiated a formal agreement with the SER that would resolve their difficulties for the time being and would define the territories of the two railways .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Under this agreement the LB&SCR would have free access to London Bridge , Bricklayers Arms station and goods yard , and Hastings .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The SER would have free use of the New Cross to Croydon line , and receive revenues from passengers at intermediate stations , but would not make or work competing lines to Brighton , Horsham , Chichester or Portsmouth .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1847 the naval dockyard of Portsmouth was being approached by two equally indirect routes from London , both under construction : a L&SWR route via Fareham and the former Brighton and Chichester Railway route from Havant .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The two companies entered into an agreement in that year to share a line from Cosham on the mainland to Portsea Island , ending at the centre of Portsmouth town .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Further progress towards the dockyard was prevented by Admiralty objections .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR began its services between Chichester and Portsmouth , on 14 June 1847 , and the L&SWR from Fareham in October 1848 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1853 the Direct Portsmouth Railway gained parliamentary authority to build a line from Godalming to Havant with the intention of the company selling itself either to the L&SWR or the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This scheme would provide a far more direct route to Portsmouth but involved sharing the LB&SCR tracks for the five miles ( 8 km ) between Havant and the joint line to Portsea .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR objected to the scheme but the L&SWR negotiated with the new company and in December 1858 sought to operate a train over the new route .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR attempted to prevent the use of its tracks and the so - called ' battle of Havant' ensued .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The matter was eventually resolved in the courts in August 1859 , and relations between the railways were formalized in agreements of 1860 and 1862 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Samuel Laing had also approved a modest degree of expansion elsewhere , most notably the acquisition of a branch line from the main line at Three Bridges to the market town of East Grinstead in July 1855 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Crystal Palace Branch Some of the directors of the LB&SCR were closely involved with the company that purchased The Crystal Palace after the completion of The Great Exhibition in October 1851 and arranged for its removal to a site on Sydenham Hill , close to the London to Brighton main line , which they purchased from Leo Schuster .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Crystal Palace became a major tourist attraction and the LB&SCR built a branch line from Sydenham to the new site , which was opened in June 1854 , and enlarged London Bridge station to handle the additional traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The attraction proved to be an enormous success with 10,000 passengers conveyed daily to and from the new branch .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On one day in 1859 , 112,000 people were conveyed to Crystal Place by train , 70,000 of which from London Bridge .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Rapid expansion 1856 – 1866 Samuel Laing retired as chairman at the end of 1855 to pursue a political career , and was replaced by the merchant banker Leo Schuster , who had previously sold his 300 - acre ( 120 ha ) estate on Sydenham Hill to the new Crystal Palace Company .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Schuster instituted a policy of rapidly expanding the route mileage of the railway with new routes throughout south London , Sussex , and east Surrey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Some of these were financed and built by the LB&SCR , others by independent local companies set up with the intention of connecting a town to the railway network with the intention of sale or lease to the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Schuster accelerated the rate of mileage increase after appointing Frederick Banister as chief engineer in 1860 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , a further 177 miles ( 285 km ) were constructed or authorised between 1857 and 1865 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: West End of London

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Schuster also encouraged an independent concern , the West End of London and Crystal Palace Railway ( WEL&CPR ) , to construct a new line extending in a wide arc round south London from the LB&SCR Crystal Palace branch to Wandsworth in 1856 and to Battersea in 1858 with a temporary terminus at Battersea Pier .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Shortly after this line was completed , the LB&SCR leased it from the WEL&CPR and incorporated it into its system .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Between 1858 and 1860 the LB&SCR was a major shareholder in the Victoria Station and Pimlico Railway ( VS&PR ) , together with the East Kent Railway ( later the London Chatham and Dover Railway ( LC&DR ) ) , the Great Western Railway ( GWR ) and the London and North Western Railway ( LNWR ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This enterprise constructed the Grosvenor Bridge over the River Thames at Battersea and the line to the Victoria Station , thereby creating a through ( albeit roundabout ) route from its main line near Croydon to a terminus in the West End of London .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Following the acquisition of the WEL&CPR , a new ' cut - off ' line between Windmill Bridge Junction ( Norwood ) and Balham was constructed during 1861 and 1862 , which reduced the distance from East Croydon to Victoria .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: New lines in South London

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The VS&PR line was also connected with another joint venture the West London Extension Joint Railway , jointly financed by the LB&SCR , L&SWR , GWR and the L&NWR , to permit goods transfers between the companies and cross-London passenger trains .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This line was opened in 1863 , and in the same year the LB&SCR and L&SWR jointly opened a large interchange station named Clapham Junction .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR also operated passenger trains between Clapham Junction and Addison Road .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The West Croydon to Wimbledon Line was built as an independent railway joining the LB&SCR and the L&SWR main lines and opened in October 1855 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: For a few months it was operated under contract by its engineer George Parker Bidder but in 1856 it was leased to the LB&SCR who purchased it in 1858 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At the same time , the LB&SCR was cooperating with the LC&DR to create the South London line between its terminuses at London Bridge and Victoria .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LC&DR was used from Victoria to Brixton , followed by new construction by the LB&SCR through Denmark Hill , and Peckham to the main line to London Bridge at South Bermondsey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: New lines in Sussex

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During 1858 , a branch line was built from Lewes to Uckfield , extended to Groombridge and Tunbridge Wells in 1868 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1864 the Newhaven branch was extended to Seaford .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The East Grinstead line was extended in 1866 to Groombridge and Tunbridge Wells .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A large area in East Sussex between Tunbridge Wells and Eastbourne remained without railways , and the LB&SCR was anxious in case the SER should venture into this territory .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , in 1864 it sought powers to build a line between these two towns , which were granted in the London , Brighton and South Coast Railway ( Additional Powers ) Act 1864 ( 27 & 28 Vict.

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: c. cccxiv ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It also obtained powers for the Ouse Valley Railway , from the south of Balcombe and north of Haywards Heath on the Brighton main line to Uckfield and Hailsham ; an extension to St Leonards was also approved by the London , Brighton , and South Coast Railway ( Saint Leonards Line ) Act 1865 ( 28 & 29 Vict. c. l ) in May 1865 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , some work had been carried out by the end of 1866 , but not completed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In West Sussex the Horsham branch was extended to Pulborough and Petworth in 1859 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1861 a line was built from near Horsham to Shoreham , providing a direct link to Brighton .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Branches were built from the West Sussex coast line to Littlehampton in 1863 , to connect with a new cross-channel ferry service , to Bognor Regis in 1864 , and to Hayling Island in 1867 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The line from Havant to Hayling had been built by the Hayling Railway , but it was leased to the LB&SCR in 1874 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Following the 1862 agreement with the L&SWR , a line was built from near Pulborough to a junction with the West Sussex coast line near Ford in 1863 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This provided a shorter LB&SCR route from London to Portsmouth via Three Bridges and Horsham .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: New lines in Surrey The Epsom and Leatherhead Railway was an independent line from the L&SW main line at Wimbledon through Epsom and Leatherhead towards Guildford .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR entered into an agreement to share its station at Epsom and to use the line as far as Leatherhead .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The line opened in August 1859 and in 1860 this portion was transferred to the joint ownership of the LB&SCR and the L&SWR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR then bought the Banstead and Epsom Downs Railway , which was building a branch line from Sutton to Epsom Downs for Epsom Downs Racecourse , opened in May 1865 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR wished to connect Horsham with significant towns in Surrey , and in 1865 it opened a line between West Horsham and the L&SWR near Guildford .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It constructed a line from Leatherhead to Dorking in March 1867 , continued to Horsham two months later .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This enabled alternative LB&SCR routes from London to Brighton and the West Sussex coast and further reduced the distance of its route from London to Portsmouth .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR supported the independent Surrey and Sussex Junction Railway , which obtained powers in July 1865 to build a line from Croydon to Tunbridge Wells via Oxted , to be worked by the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The involvement of LB&SCR directors in this scheme was interpreted by the SER as a breach of the 1849 agreement , and in retaliation the SER and LC&DR obtained the South Eastern and London , Chatham and Dover ( London , Lewes and Brighton ) Railways Act 1866 ( 29 & 30 Vict.

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: c. cccxviii ) for a rival ' London , Lewes and Brighton Railway ' , which would undermine the profitable LB&SCR monopoly to that town .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Neither scheme was proceeded with .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Newhaven Harbour Following the opening of the branch from Lewes to Newhaven , the LB&SCR sought to develop a shorter Continental route from London to Paris via Dieppe , in competition with the SER routes from Dover to Calais and Folkestone to Boulogne .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR built its wharf and warehousing facilities on the east side of the river , with Newhaven Harbour station .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It funded the dredging of the channel and other improvements to the harbour between 1850 and 1878 , to enable it to be used by larger cross-channel ferries , and in 1863 the LB&SCR and the Chemins de Fer de l'Ouest introduced the Newhaven – Dieppe passenger service .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1878 the railway formed and underwrote the Newhaven Harbour Company and thereafter delegated responsibility for its operation to it .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Growth of the London suburbs

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Largely as a result of the railway , the rural area between New Cross and Croydon rapidly became built up , and the population of Croydon increased 14 - fold , from 16,700 to 233,000 , during the LB&SCR 's existence .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the 1860s the LB&SCR began to develop new traffic from the growing number of middle - class commuters who were beginning to live in the south London suburbs and working in central London .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As part of its suburban expansion , the LB&SCR built a line from Peckham Rye roughly parallel to the main line , through East Dulwich , Tulse Hill , Streatham and Mitcham to Sutton and Epsom Downs , which opened in October 1868 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Deterioration of relations with the SER Relations between the LB&SCR and the SER and the interpretation of the 1848 agreement continued to be difficult throughout the 1850s and 1860s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: They reached a low point in 1863 when the SER produced a report for its shareholders outlining a long list of the difficulties between the two companies , and the reasons why they considered that the LB&SCR had broken the 1848 agreement .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main areas of disagreement listed were at Hastings , allowing the LC&DR to use its lines to Victoria , a proposed LB&SCR branch to Bromley , the new LB&SCR line to Dorking , LB&SCR opposition to the SER attempts at building a line to the west end , the LB&SCR agreement to let the LC&DR use its goods facilities at Bricklayers Arms , and the perennial problem of the shared main line between Redhill and Croydon .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The most flagrant example of the lack of cooperation between the two companies , however , was with respect to the independent Caterham Railway , which ran in South Eastern territory , but joined the Brighton mainline at the LB&SCR Godstone Road station ( later renamed Caterham Junction ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Both companies objected to the other operating the branch line , which resulted in a delay of a year between the completion of the work and the opening of the line in 1856 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Their failure to agree on such matters as through ticketing quickly drove the independent company into bankruptcy .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway
