text: 1867 financial crisis and its impact

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The collapse of the bankers Overend , Gurney and Company in 1866 and the financial crisis the following year brought the LB&SCR to the brink of bankruptcy .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A special meeting of shareholders was adjourned , and the powers of the board of directors were suspended pending receipt of a report into the financial affairs of the company and its prospects .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The report made clear that the LB&SCR had overextended itself with large capital projects sustained by profits from passengers , which suddenly declined as a result of the crisis .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Several country lines were losing money – most notably between Horsham and Guildford , East Grinstead and Tunbridge Wells , and Banstead and Epsom – and the LB&SCR was committed to building or acquiring others with equally poor prospects .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The report was extremely critical of the policies of Schuster and the company secretary , Frederick Slight , both of whom resigned .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It did however point out that these lines had been built or acquired as a means for preventing competition from neighbouring railways .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The committee recommended the abandonment of several projects , and that the LB&SCR should enter into a working agreement with the SER .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The new board of directors accepted many of these recommendations , and they managed to persuade Samuel Laing to return as chairman .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was through his business acumen and that of the new secretary and general manager J. P. Knight that the LB&SCR gradually recovered its financial health during the early 1870s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , all construction of lines was suspended .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Three important projects then under construction were abandoned : the Ouse Valley Railway , its extension to St Leonards , and the Surrey and Sussex Junction Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The line between Tunbridge Wells and Eastbourne was shelved until the financial situation improved .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: For the next decade , projects were limited to additional spurs or junctions in London and Brighton to enhance the operation of the network , or small - scale ventures in conjunction with other railway companies .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The latter included a short line from Streatham through Tooting to Wimbledon in 1868 , and a connection from Portsmouth Town to Portsmouth Harbour in 1876 , both jointly with the L&SWR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The proposed ' working cooperation ' with the SER never took effect but remained under active consideration by both parties , and later involved the LC&DR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was not until 1875 that the idea was dropped , after the SER pulled out of negotiations due to the conditions imposed by Parliament on the proposed merger .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR continued as an independent railway but the SER and LCDR eventually formed a working relationship in 1899 with the formation of the South Eastern and Chatham Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: One new line to which the LB&SCR was committed was the East London Railway , a consortium of six railway companies : the Great Eastern Railway ( GER ) ; the LB&SCR ; the LC&DR ; the SER ; the Metropolitan Railway ; and the District Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It sought to reuse the Thames Tunnel , built by Marc and Isambard Kingdom Brunel between 1825 and 1843 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A line was therefore built between the LB&SCR at New Cross and Wapping with a link to the GER main line , in March 1869 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was primarily intended for goods transfer between these railways , but the LB&SCR introduced a passenger service between Liverpool Street Station and Croydon .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Later 19th century

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By the mid-1870s the LB&SCR had recovered its financial stability through a policy of encouraging the more intensive use of lines and reducing operating costs .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Between 1870 and 1889 annual revenue rose from £ 1.3 million to £ 2.4 million , whilst its operating costs rose from £ 650,000 to just over £ 1 million .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was able to embark upon new railway building and improvements to infrastructure .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Some new lines passed through sparsely populated areas and merely provided shorter connections to towns that were already on the railway network , and so were unlikely to be profitable , but the LB&SCR found itself under pressure from local communities wanting a rail connection , and was frightened that they would otherwise be developed by rivals .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main reason for the financial recovery lay in the exploitation of London suburban traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By the late 1880s the LB&SCR had developed the largest suburban network of any British railway , with 68 route miles ( 109 km ) in the suburbs in addition to its main lines , in three routes between London Bridge and Victoria : the South London line , the outer South London Line and the Crystal Palace lines , and the LB&SCR was earning more from season tickets than any other British railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Thus an official return showed that the railway had operated more than 100,000 passenger trains from April to June 1889 , more than any other company operating only in southern England .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: New routes and station improvements

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The scheme to link Eastbourne with Tunbridge Wells was revived in April 1879 with the opening of a line connecting the Hailsham branch to Heathfield , completed the following September from Heathfield to Eridge , and later known as the Cuckoo Line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Authority was granted to the Lewes and East Grinstead Railway ( L&EGR ) by the Lewes and East Grinstead Railway Act 1877 ( 40 & 41 Vict. c. ccxviii ) , to build a line roughly parallel to the ' Cuckoo Line ' , sponsored by local landowners , including the Earl of Sheffield , and including a branch from Horsted Keynes to Haywards Heath on the Brighton main line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A year later the London , Brighton , and South Coast Railway ( Croydon , Oxted , and East Grinstead Railways ) Act 1878 ( 41 & 42 Vict. c. lxxii ) enabled the LB&SCR to acquire and operate lines , opened in August 1882 and September 1883 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The East Grinstead – Lewes line subsequently became known as the ' Bluebell line ' and , following its closure in 1958 , the section between Horsted Keynes and Sheffield Park was taken over by the Bluebell Railway Preservation Society .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR in West Sussex was largely complete by 1870 except for a link between Midhurst and Chichester , delayed by the financial crisis of 1867 ; this was revived and opened in 1881 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Minor improvements around Littlehampton were made , and a branch to Devil 's Dyke opened in 1887 , built by and owned by an independent company but operated by the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In Hampshire the LB&SCR leased the Hayling Island branch line from 1874 , opened in 1865 as an independent concern .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR and the L&SWR jointly built a 1+1⁄4 - mile ( 2 km ) branch from a new station on their existing joint line at Fratton to East Southsea in 1887 , but early in the 20th century had to compete with a tramway , and it was closed at the outbreak of the First World War in August 1914 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Although the proposed Surrey and Sussex Junction Railway had been abandoned in 1867 , there remained a demand from Croydon to towns such as East Grinstead , Tunbridge Wells and the East Sussex coast .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The SER was looking for a relief route in the same general direction for its Tonbridge and Hastings services , and the two railways collaborated in a joint line between South Croydon , on the main Brighton line , and Oxted .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Beyond Oxted , the LB&SCR would build its own lines to link with the Bluebell line at East Grinstead and its line to Tunbridge Wells .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: SER trains would join the line between Redhill and Tonbridge .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Authority was granted in 1878 and they opened in 1884 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Brighton railway station was rebuilt and extended in 1882 – 83 with a new single roof , and Eastbourne was rebuilt in 1886 to cope with additional traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Congestion and slow trains

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: With the steady growth of traffic in the South London suburbs during the 1880s and early 1890s , the LB&SCR was the subject of press criticism for poor timekeeping and slow trains , although it was never subjected to the levels of press and public obloquy accorded to the SER .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Two of the reasons for poor timekeeping were the volume of traffic generated and the complexity of the LB&SCR network north of Redhill with large numbers of junctions and signals .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A further complication was that both the LB&SCR and the SER shared the 11 miles ( 18 km ) of track between Redhill and East Croydon .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This part of the line was owned by the SER , which ( according to Acworth ) gave its trains precedence through the junctions at Redhill , but the LB&SCR paid an annual fee of £ 14,000 for its use .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Relations with the SER began to deteriorate once more and eventually both companies appointed Henry Oakley general manager of the Great Northern Railway as an independent assessor in 1889 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Oakley supported the LB&SCR right to use the line but increased the annual payment to £ 20,000 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However this did not solve the problem and an 1896 study of LB&SCR passenger services , by J. Pearson Pattinson described the 8+1⁄4 miles ( 13.3 km ) of shared track between Redhill and Stoats Nest ( Coulsdon ) as being ' in a state of the utmost congestion , and detentions of the Brighton expresses , blocked by South Eastern stopping trains , are as constant as irritating . '

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Quarry line Ultimately the only solution was for the LB&SCR to build its own line between Coulsdon North and Earlswood , bypassing Redhill , which became known as the ' Quarry line ' .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Plans were drawn up by Charles L. Morgan , the chief engineer .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Authority was granted by Parliament in July 1896 , and construction took place in 1898 – 99 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The line involved substantial civil engineering works including the excavation of new tunnels at Merstham and Redhill , cuttings , embankments and a covered way at Cane Hill Hospital .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The line opened on 8 November 1899 ( 1 April 1900 for passengers ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: 20th century During its last 20 years the LB&SCR opened no new lines , but invested in improving its main line and London terminals , together with the electrification of its London suburban services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Following the completion of the Quarry line , the bottleneck on the heavily used main line moved further south .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Plans were drawn up for the quadrupling throughout , but only the 16 miles ( 26 km ) from Earlswood to Three Bridges were completed , between 1906 and 1909 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A fifth track was laid between Norwood Junction and South Croydon in 1907 – 08 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Extension beyond Three Bridges would have involved heavy engineering at Balcombe tunnel , over the Ouse Valley Viaduct and through the South Downs .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The required capital expenditure was diverted to extending the electrification programme .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Unlike other mainline railway companies , the LB&SCR had to share both its London termini with its rivals , London Bridge with the SER and Victoria with the LC&DR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The rapid increase in commuting towards the end of the 19th century created an urgent need to expand the cramped and limited facilities at Victoria .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the first decade of the new century the line between Grosvenor Bridge and Victoria was widened and the station rebuilt on a much larger scale .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A new turntable and locomotive servicing facilities enabled the use of more powerful locomotives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the same period LB&SCR facilities at London Bridge were enlarged , but since the station had been rebuilt so many times it remained a ' sprawling confusion ' .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Motive power shortage Between 1905 and 1912 the LB&SCR suffered an increasingly serious motive power shortage due to the inability of Brighton Works to keep pace with the volume of repairs and new construction required .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By 1910 30 % of the locomotive stock was unusable due to delays and inefficiencies at the works , leading to the sickness and retirement of the Locomotive , Carriage and Wagon Superintendent D. E. Marsh .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The problem was solved by the establishment of Lancing Carriage Works and the reorganisation of Brighton Works by Marsh 's successor L. B. Billinton .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The First World War

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: With other British railways the LB&SCR was brought under government control during the First World War .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Until then it had carried relatively little heavy goods , but this changed dramatically at the outbreak of war .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was responsible for carrying the bulk of the stores and munitions delivered to the British troops on the continent , principally through its port of Newhaven

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This included nearly 7 million tons of goods , including 2.7 million tons of explosives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It necessitated an additional 53,376 goods trains over the four years of the war .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Newhaven harbour also received casualties landing in hospital ships , with the railway providing ambulance trains .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were several army camps within the territory of the LB&SCR which therefore provided 27,366 troop trains .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Army horses awaiting shipping to France were stabled at Farlington Racecourse .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At the outbreak of hostilities the area surrounding Newhaven Port was requisitioned and the Harbour station closed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: From 22 September 1916 Newhaven became a special military area for handling Government traffic under the Defence of the Realm Regulations .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This additional traffic required substantial improvements to infrastructure , notably at Newhaven harbour , where additional warehousing , new sidings and signalling constructed and electric lighting was installed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: When Newhaven became overwhelmed the tidal port of Littlehampton was rebuilt and pressed into service .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Inland , a much enlarged goods marshalling yard was established at Three Bridges , which was chosen as a nodal point for handling War traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At Gatwick and Haywards Heath , passing loops were constructed so that the frequent passenger trains would not be impeded by slower goods trains and to hold munitions trains during air raids .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Some munitions trains were routed to Newhaven via the Steyning Line to Brighton to avoid congesting the part of the Brighton main line which had only two tracks .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Between 1914 and 1918 , 5,635 members of LB&SCR staff joined the forces , creating staff shortages at all levels ( including the Chief Mechanical Engineer who was called up for service in Russia and Romania ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This necessitated the employment of female labour in clerical grades and for carriage cleaning .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The railway erected a War Memorial at London Bridge in 1920 honouring the 532 staff who had lost their lives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Likewise , in April 1922 , the last locomotive to be constructed by the company , 4- 6 - 4T ' L ' Class No. 333 , was named ' Remembrance ' and carried a memorial plaque .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: LB&SCR at Grouping By 31 December 1922 , when the LB&SCR ceased to have an independent existence , it had 457 miles ( 735 km ) of route .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Of these , 100 mi ( 161 km ) was single track , 357 mi ( 575 km ) double track , 47 mi ( 76 km ) triple track , and 49 mi ( 79 km ) four or more tracks .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Sidings had a total length of 355 miles ( 571 km ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: According to Bonavia , ' the Brighton was a highly individual line in its strengths and weaknesses , it was to experience drastic changes under Southern [ Railway ] management which older members of the staff would not always accept gracefully . '

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Train services

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was essentially a passenger - carrying concern , with goods and mineral traffic playing a limited role in its receipts .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As originally envisaged the railway was a trunk route , conveying passengers ( and to a lesser extent goods ) between London , Croydon and the south coast , with relatively little traffic to and from stations in between .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , the railway 's existence began to generate new goods and passenger traffic at towns and villages on or near the main line , such as Reigate , Crawley and Haywards Heath .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This also applied to Sussex and Surrey market towns such as Lewes , Horsham , East Grinstead and Dorking as soon as these were connected to the rail network .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: After 1870 the development of the London suburbs south of the Thames had a profound effect on the nature of the railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The development of Newhaven harbour was also a stimulus to the development of both categories of traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The speed and punctuality of many LB&SCR passenger services was the subject of widespread criticism in the technical and popular press during the 1890s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This was in part due in part to the complexity of the system between London and Croydon , with a large number of signals and junctions , the sharing of stretches of line with the SER , and the relatively short routes , which gave little opportunity to make up for lost time .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR gradually began to rebuild its reputation during the 20th century through improvements to mainline infrastructure and electrification of suburban services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Express passenger services

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The company had no long - distance express trains , with a maximum journey length of 75 miles ( 121 km ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Nevertheless , frequent express passenger services ran to the most important coastal destinations from both London Bridge and Victoria .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Season ticket revenue , particularly from Brighton to London , was the backbone of the LB&SCR 's finances for most of the 19th century .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The morning rush hour business services were among " the heaviest express services in the world " in the 1880s , with loads of 360 tons .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Individual Pullman cars were introduced to Britain on the Midland Railway in 1874 , followed by the Great Northern Railway soon after and the LB&SCR in 1875 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR pioneered all - Pullman trains in England , the Pullman Limited Express on 5 December 1881 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It consisted of four cars built at the Pullman Car Company workshops in Derby , Beatrice , Louise , Maud and Victoria , the first electrically lit coaches on a British railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The train made two down and two up trips per day , one each way on Sundays .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was renamed the Brighton Pullman Limited in 1887 , and first - class carriages were attached .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A new train was built in 1888 : three Pullmans were shipped over in parts from the Pullman Palace Car Company in America , and assembled by the LB&SCR at Brighton .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Brighton Limited was introduced on 2 October 1898 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It ran only on Sundays , and not in July – September .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was timed to make the journey from Victoria in 60 minutes : " London to Brighton in one hour " was the advertisement used for the first time .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 21 December 1902 it made a record run of 54 minutes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It hit the headlines again when , faced with the threat of a competing electric railway being built from London to Brighton , it ran to Brighton in 48 minutes 41 seconds and the return to London in 50 minutes 21 seconds , matching the schedule put forward by the promoters of the electric line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Southern Belle , introduced 8 November 1908 , was described as " the most luxurious train in the World . "

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By 1910 two trips each way were running every day ; later three were run on Sundays .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Third - class Pullman cars began running on Sunday 12 September 1915 from Victoria to Brighton and Eastbourne .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stopping trains Slower passenger services between London and the south coast often divided at East Croydon to serve both the London termini , and combined there for down trains , so East Croydon had an important nodal function in the system .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: After 1867 , following the opening of the direct line to Horsham , Sutton acted as a similar node for passenger trains between London and Portsmouth .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Slip coaches

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR appears to have invented the practice of slipping coaches from the rear of express trains at intermediate stations for onward transmission to branch lines or smaller stations on the main line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The earliest recorded example was at Haywards Heath in February 1858 , where coaches for Hastings were slipped from a London – Brighton express .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The slipping was coordinated by a series of communication bell signals between the guards on the two portions of the train and the locomotive crew .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Before 1914 , twenty - one coaches were slipped each day on the Brighton main line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Coaches were slipped at Horley and Three Bridges for stations to East Grinstead , Forest Row and Horsham , or at Haywards Heath for stations to Brighton and Eastbourne .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The practice continued until the electrification of the main line in 1932 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: London suburban traffic After 1870 , the LB&SCR greatly encouraged commuters into London by reducing the prices of season tickets and introducing special workmen 's trains for manual workers in that year .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By May 1890 the company was operating 10,773 trains into its London termini each month , more than any other company .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This growth changed the character of the railway and had a profound influence upon its motive power policy and passenger train services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In the 1870s and 1880s it led to the building of new standard tank engine classes such as the Terrier and D1 classes under William Stroudley .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: R. J. Billinton replaced these with the D3 , E3 , E4 , and E5 classes designed for London suburban services , during the 1890s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: When steam locomotives became unable to cope with the increased suburban traffic and competition from electric trams in the early 20th century , it resulted in the electrification of the London suburban network .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Excursion and holiday traffic

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Excursion trains from London to the South Coast and the Sussex countryside had been introduced in 1844 , and were a feature of the LB&SCR throughout its existence .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Special fares to Brighton and other south coast resorts on summer Sundays and at bank holidays were regularly advertised in the press .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Likewise , special trains serving the regular fetes and exhibitions at Crystal Palace during the summer months .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: After 1870 the LB&SCR sought to develop the holiday and excursion trade and market other south coast resorts such as Hayling Island and the Isle of Wight as holiday destinations , by publishing a range of attractive posters .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On the Isle of Wight the LB&SCR and the L&SWR jointly took over the ferry service from Portsmouth and built new pier at Ryde with a short line to the station at St John 's Road in 1880 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the 1900s the company ran special Sunday trains to enable London cyclists to explore the Sussex and Surrey countryside .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By 1905 the railway was offering day trips to Dieppe and circular tickets , valid for a month , to enable Londoners to explore towns along the South Coast .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1904 the Great Western Railway inaugurated holiday trains during the summer months from Birkenhead to Brighton and Eastbourne , in conjunction with the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The following year LB&SCR and L&NWR jointly operated the Sunny South Special from Liverpool and Manchester to these destinations .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: These trains operated via the West London lines , with the LB&SCR responsible for their operation from Kensington or Willesden .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR served important Horse racing tracks at Brighton , Epsom , Gatwick , Goodwood , Lewes , Lingfield and Plumpton , and Portsmouth Park ( Farlington ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Race day special trains were an important source of revenue during the summer months .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Rail motor services During the first few years of the 20th century the LB&SCR , in common with other railways , became concerned about losses on branch and short - distance passenger services , particularly in winter .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The L&SWR and the LB&SCR boards decided to investigate the use of steam powered railcars on the 1+1⁄4 - mile ( 2 km ) joint branch line between Fratton and East Southsea , in June 1903 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The locomotive and carriage units were both built by the L&SWR , but one of the carriages was painted in the LB&SCR livery .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The two vehicles had to be quickly withdrawn as they were found to be chronically underpowered , but were rebuilt with larger boilers and thereafter gave adequate service .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , their use did not stem the loss of traffic to the roads and in 1914 the branch was closed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Nevertheless , the LB&SCR directors asked the Chief Mechanical Engineer , Robert Billinton , to investigate the use of steam or petrol railcars on lightly used services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Billinton died in 1904 , before examples could be acquired , but in 1905 his successor Douglas Earle Marsh acquired two steam railcars from Beyer , Peacock and Company and two petrol railcars from Dick , Kerr & Co .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: These were compared with small steam locomotives of the Stroudley A1 and D1 classes fitted for " motor train " or " push - pull " working .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Neither type of railcar was successful , being inadequate to cope with traffic fluctuations between winter and summer , but the " motor trains " could be adapted by the addition or removal of extra coaches .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , the experiment provided a new lease of life for the Stroudley tank classes , which continued to be used on branch lines for many years after their withdrawal from suburban services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The steam railcars were sold in 1919 , and the petrol railcars were used for departmental ( non-revenue - earning ) purposes during the erection of the catenary for the overhead electrification of the London suburban lines .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the experiments relating to railcars and motor trains , the LB&SCR constructed unmanned halts , such as Lyons Crossing Halt and Littlehaven Halt on the Arun Valley Line , in an attempt to increase passenger revenue .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Freight services Freight represented a relatively small part of the LB&SCR 's finances during its first half century .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Agricultural goods and general merchandise were carried , together with wine , foodstuffs and manufactured goods imported from France .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the 1870s the pattern of goods services slowly began to change , leading to rapid growth in the 1890s , ' caused by the transport of raw materials and finished products of entirely new industries such as petroleum , cement , brick and tile manufacture , forestry and biscuit making . '

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This resulted in the construction of 55 goods locomotives of the C2 class

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were no coal mines within LB&SCR territory , and so it had to pay substantially more for its fuel than most other companies .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The bulk of its coal was brought in 800 long tons ( 810 t ) trains from Acton yard on the Great Western Railway to Three Bridges for redistribution , and the LB&SCR kept two goods locomotives at the GWR Westbourne Park Depot for this purpose .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1898 there was a scheme to develop Deptford Wharf for the landing of coal by sea .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The additional fuel costs were partially offset by the sale of shingle for rail ballast from Pevensey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main London goods depot was at ' Willow Walk ' , part of the Bricklayers Arms complex , where the LB&SCR established its facilities in 1849 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: These were enlarged in 1854 after it entered into an agreement with the LC&DR to handle its goods traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Further extensions were built in 1865 and 1902 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were also freight handling facilities at Battersea and Deptford Wharves , and New Cross in London and the railway constructed a marshalling yard to the south of Norwood Junction during the 1870s , extended in the early 1880s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Other freight handling facilities outside London were at : Brighton ( where there was a separate goods station at , adjacent to the passenger station ) , Eastbourne , Hastings , Littlehampton , Portsmouth , Newhaven , Seaford , and Three Bridges .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Proposals for a London and Brighton Electric Railway made to Parliament in 1900 failed to proceed , but caused the LB&SCR to consider electrification .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Also , competition from the introduction of trams in London meant that annual traffic over the circuitous 8+1⁄2 - mile ( 14 km ) route between Victoria and London Bridge stations had dropped from 8 million to 3 million journeys by 1908 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Because of the nature of its traffic with a very large number of commuter journeys over relatively short distances , the railway was an obvious candidate for electrification , and had sought powers for suburban lines in 1903 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Third and fourth rail direct current electrification had been chosen for the underground tube railways and the Metropolitan Railway and District Railway in London , the Mersey Railway in Liverpool and the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Liverpool to Southport line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However the LB&SCR foresaw electrification of its main line , and ultimately to Portsmouth and Hastings , and therefore decided on a high - tension overhead supply system at 6,600 V 25 Hz AC .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Although the Midland Railway line from Lancaster to Morecambe and Heysham had been the first to use overhead lines , the LB&SCR lines covered a far greater length of track .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This system was of German origin and the contractor for the electrical equipment was Allgemeine Elektricitäts Gesellschaft of Berlin , while the main contractor was Robert W Blackwell & Co Ltd .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Power supply was from the London Electric Supply Corporation ( LESCo ) at Deptford .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The first section was the South London line connecting London Bridge with Victoria via Denmark Hill , opened on 1 December 1909 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was marketed as ' The Elevated Electric ' and was an immediate success .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Traffic on the line grew from 3 to 10 million journeys per year .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Other routes followed : on 12 May 1911 Victoria – Crystal Palace via Balham and West Norwood , followed on 3 March 1912 by the line from Peckham Rye to West Norwood .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Repair shops were established at Peckham Rye , and carriage sheds at Norwood Junction .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At opening the rolling stock consisted of 16 motor coaches these were supplemented by an additional of 30 motor coaches in 1911 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Continued success and profitability of its earliest projects caused the LB&SCR to decide to electrify all remaining London suburban lines in 1913 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , the outbreak of war the following year delayed what was planned to have been considerable further mileage of electrified line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By 1921 most of the inner London suburban lines were electrified , and during 1922 lines to Coulsdon North and Sutton , opened on 1 April 1925 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During 1920 , plans were drawn up to extend the ' Elevated Electric ' to Brighton , Worthing , Eastbourne , Newhaven and Seaford , and to Epsom and Oxted , but these were overtaken by the Grouping .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The ' Elevated Electric ' proved to be a technical and financial success , but was short - lived since the L&SWR had adopted the third - rail system : it s mileage far exceeded that of the LB&SCR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1926 the Southern Railway announced that , as part of a huge electrification project , all overhead lines were to be converted to third rail , thus bringing all lines into a common system .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The last overhead electric train ran on 22 September 1929 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Accidents and signalling control Semaphore signalling and signal boxes were first introduced on the L&CR and had been adopted by the L&BR as early as the 1840s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were a number of serious accidents in the early years of the LB&SCR , some due to failures in communication .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR began to improve its safety record in the 1860s with the introduction of interlocking , and the early introduction of Westinghouse air brakes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Given the large number of junctions and the intensive use of its system , the LB&SCR maintained a good safety record during the last half century of its existence .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The following accidents occurred on the LB&SCR :

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 6 June 1851 , there was a derailment at Falmer Bank , East Sussex due to an object on the line .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 27 November 1851 , passenger train from Brighton ran into the eighth wagon of a goods train that had just left Ford , station , West Sussex , due to the passenger train passing a signal at danger .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 17 March 1853 , the boiler of locomotive No. 10 exploded at Brighton , East Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 27 August 1853 , confusion over a warning signal at New Cross caused a goods train to collide with an empty passenger train , resulting in the death of a fireman On 21 August 1854 , there was an accident at East Croydon , Surrey due to numerous causes , resulting in three fatalities and eleven injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 3 October 1859 , the boiler of a locomotive exploded at Falmer Incline .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 25 August 1861 , in the accident known as the Clayton Tunnel rail crash , an excursion train ran into the rear of another inside Clayton Tunnel , West Sussex due to a combination of the failure of an automatic signal to return to ' danger ' and culpable operating errors .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: At the time , this was the deadliest accident up to that time in the United Kingdom with 23 people killed and 176 people injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 29 May 1863 , there was a derailment at Streatham Common , Surrey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Four people ( including the driver ) were killed 59 people were injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 23 June 1869 , two trains collided at New Cross Gate , Surrey due to driver error , excessive speed and guard error , injuring 91 people .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 27 September 1879 , the boiler of a locomotive exploded at Lewes , East Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: One person was killed and two were injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 1 May 1891 , in the accident known as the Norwood Junction rail accident , a cast-iron bridge collapsed under a train at Norwood Junction , Surrey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Six people were injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 23 July 1894 , a brake van next to the engine hauling the 6.35 pm from Havant derailed at Farlington Halt railway station and the first two coaches overturned .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The guard on the train was killed and seven passengers were injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 1 September 1897 , a passenger train derailed near Heathfield , East Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: One person was killed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 23 December 1899 , a Brighton train passed a signal at danger and ran into the back of a boat train express in thick fog at Keymer Junction , West Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were six fatalities and 20 injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1904 , a freight train hauled by D1 class No. 239 Patcham was derailed at Cocking , West Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 29 January 1910 , an express passenger train became divided and was derailed at Stoat 's Nest , Surrey due to a defective wheelset on a carriage .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Seven people were killed and 65 were injured .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 21 October 1913 , seven labourers were working a night shift at London Bridge station , scraping and cleaning the cradles and insulator fittings of the overhead line equipment .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The wire brush of one of the men , labourer Amos Boniface , touched one of the electrical wires and he suffered severe burns .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Boniface died 19 days later from his injuries .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 3 April 1916 , a passenger train was derailed between Crowborough & Jarvis Brook and Buxted stations , East Sussex .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On 18 April 1918 , a freight train became divided , the rear part coming to rest inside Redhill Tunnel , Surrey .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Due to a signalman 's error , another freight train ran into the wagons and was derailed .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A third freight train ran into the wreckage .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Signalling and signal boxes

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR originally used semaphore for home signals and ' double disc ' for distant signals , but after 1872 semaphore signals were used for both purposes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR was using primitive interlocking between signals at some junctions by 1844 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1856 , John Saxby , an LB&SCR carpenter , patented a form of manual interlocking of the points and signals , first tried at Bricklayers Arms that year .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The first fully interlocking frame was installed by Saxby at Keymer Junction near Haywards Heath in 1860 , where he built a small workshop to undertake private work .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: He left the company and in 1862 formed Saxby & Farmer signalling contractors .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Thereafter the LB&SC patronised Saxby & Farmer for most of its signalling until circa 1880 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Thereafter it adopted the Sykes ' Lock and block ' system used on the LC&DR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR inherited the world 's first signal boxes , at Bricklayers Arms Junction and Brighton Junction ( Norwood ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: After 1880 it gradually developed its own architecture for signal boxes , using home - produced and contractor - built frames .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: J. E. Annett , the inventor of Annett 's key in 1875 , a portable form of interlocking , was a former LB&SCR employee .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the remodelling of London Victoria station between 1898 and 1908 it was resignalled using the Sykes electromechanical method for controlling points and signals , allowing for more compact signal boxes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Rolling stock

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: For the greater part of its existence the LB&SCR relied upon steam locomotives for motive power , and it owned no diesel or electric locomotives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The electrified lines were worked by electric multiple units for passenger traffic and by steam for freight .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It experimented with two petrol railcars in 1906 and 1907 , but these proved to be underpowered and highly unreliable and were soon taken out of traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR under Stroudley was one of the first railways in Britain to adopt the Westinghouse air brake after 1877 in preference to the far less effective vacuum brakes employed by its neighbours .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Steam locomotives

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR inherited 51 steam locomotives from the Brighton , Croydon and Dover Joint Committee , and it built or purchased 1,055 locomotives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Of these , 620 were handed over to the Southern Railway on 1 January 1923 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR achieved early fame as the first railway to use the Jenny Lind 2 - 2 - 2 locomotive in 1847 , designed by David Joy , the Chief Draughtsman of the E. B. Wilson and Company of Leeds , later widely used by other railways .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The policy of John Chester Craven , Locomotive Superintendent from 1847 to 1869 , was to design locomotives for each task or type of traffic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Many of his designs were capable locomotives , but with 72 different classes in use at the time of William Stroudley 's appointment in 1870 , the policy was hopelessly uneconomic .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stroudley reduced this to 12 main classes , many with interchangeable parts , by 1888 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: He introduced a number of extremely successful and long - lived designs , notably the A1 ( ' Terrier ' ) and E1 classes 0 - 6 - 0T , and the D1 class 0 - 4 - 2T , the powerful G class 2 - 2 - 2 ' singles ' and the B1 ' Gladstone ' class 0 - 4 - 2 express passenger locomotives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Less successful were his C and C1 0 - 6 - 0 classes of 1871 and 1882 respectively , both of which proved to be underpowered as the volume of freight traffic grew towards the end of the century .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stroudley 's locomotives were all limited to six wheels , and he never used bogies largely because of the limitations imposed by turntables , notably at Victoria .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The high price of coal encouraged him to experiment with condensing apparatus .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stroudley 's successor R. J. Billinton continued the process of standardisation of locomotive parts until his death in 1904 , thereby reducing maintenance costs .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: He introduced eight - wheeled designs in the form of 4 - 4 - 0 express locomotives of the B4 class and the D3 class 0 - 4 - 4T , for use on London suburban services .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: He also introduced a very successful and versatile series of four 0 - 6 - 2T tank engine classes with radial axles for both passenger and freight duties .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Of less success was his 0 - 6 - 0 freight locomotives of the C2 class .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: D.E. Marsh continued the process of building larger locomotives with the H1 class of 4 - 4 - 2 express passenger locomotives of 1905 , based on a former Great Northern railway design .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A superheated version was introduced in 1911 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Marsh was also responsible for the design of four of 4 - 4 - 2T classes ( I1 - I4 ) but of these , only the I3 class were successful , being described by Klaus Marx as ' wonder engines ' .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This class was also instrumental in demonstrating the benefits of superheating to locomotive engineers in Britain .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Marsh also designed a class of 4 - 6 - 2 tank engines , and a very poor C3 class of 0 - 6 - 0 , freight locomotives , which proved to perform worse than the locomotives they were due to replace .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: However , he found that by rebuilding Billinton 's unsuccessful C2 class with his newly designed C3 boiler he was at last able to produce a successful freight design for the railway in the form of the C2X class .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The last Chief Mechanical Engineer was L.B. Billinton , who designed the powerful K class 2 - 6 - 0 mixed - traffic locomotives and the LB&SCR E2 class in 1913 , and the L class 4 - 6 - 4 tanks of 1914 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: All of these designs were successful but his career was cut short by the First World War and the grouping of British railways .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: According to D.L. Bradley , the railway handed over " a nicely balanced stock of locomotives well - suited to the demands of the Brighton section " to the Southern Railway at grouping in 1923 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: LB&SCR locomotive designs had little impact on the locomotive policy of the Southern Railway after 1923 because they were built to a more generous loading gauge and had Westinghouse air brakes unlike the two other main constituent companies .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Although the designs were not perpetuated , the originals proved to be particularly long - lived .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: 62.8 % of locomotives inherited by the Southern Railway were still in use at the nationalisation of British Railways in 1948 , compared with 57.9 % for the L&SWR and 56.8 % for the SE&CR .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Electric traction

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The electrified lines were operated by electric multiple units .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: These were originally three - car units , with a trailer sandwiched between motor cars , later converted into two - car units with one driving motor car and one driving trailer .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: New classes of multiple unit were developed for each electrified line , known as the South London stock and the Crystal Palace stock .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A third type , the Coulsdon and Wallington stock was planned by the LB&SCR but introduced by the Southern Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Coaching stock

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The jobs of Locomotive Superintendent and Carriage and wagon superintendent were combined until the retirement of D. E. Marsh in 1911 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , the LB&SCR was never at the forefront of carriage development for its ordinary coaching stock , and as late as the mid-1860s was still building open - side 3rd class carriages .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stroudley introduced four - wheeled and later six - wheeled designs which lasted for 40 years , and shortly before his death in 1889 he introduced a few bogie carriages for the main business trains .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stroudley was a pioneer of dynamo - driven electric lighting and communication cords .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR introduced breakfast cars to its main business trains .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The appointment of Albert Panter as Carriage and Wagon Works Manager under Robert Billinton in 1898 ( Carriage and Wagon Superintendent from 1912 ) led to the introduction of bogie carriages for mainline trains in 1905 , but suburban services were operated by six -wheeled " block trains " with solid wooden buffers , permanently tight coupled in sets of ten or 12 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Many of these were still in use at grouping in 1923 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Better vehicles appeared early in the 20th century with the ' Balloon stock ' and electric stock .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Sixteen carriages of LB&SCR origin have been preserved , including one luxurious " Directors ' saloon " of 1914 : these are principally on the Bluebell Railway and the Isle of Wight Steam Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A number of grounded carriage bodies used as holiday homes survive .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Wagons Sixteen wagons formerly in LB&SCR ownership now survive , largely because the Southern Railway transferred them to the Isle of Wight , where they remained in use until the 1960s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Liveries After 1870 the LB&SCR was renowned for the attractiveness of its locomotives and coaching stock and condition of its country stations .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: " No company , even the North - Western itself turns out smarter looking trains than the Brighton main line expresses and even some of the suburban trains . "

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Between 1846 and 1870 passenger locomotives were painted hunter green with some having black lining .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Frames were red , and wheels were black ; buffer beams were the regulation ' signal red ' .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Goods locomotives were black with red and white lining , except those operating into Brighton or London Bridge , in passenger livery .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Some engines had boilers lagged with wooden strips .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: These were either highly polished mahogany with brass fixings or were painted in alternating stripes of dark green and vermilion .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The main shade of green used gradually became darker .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By the time Stroudley became Locomotive Superintendent the colour had become a variant of Brunswick Green used by many other companies .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Carriages were painted sea green or varnished wood , the latter mainly first class stock .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: From 1870 to 1905 the livery was Stroudley 's famous Improved Engine Green , a golden ochre very similar to that used by his former employer , the Highland Railway .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: On passenger locomotives Improved Engine Green was finished with olive green borders lined with black , red and white .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Frames and buffer beams were carmine red , lined with yellow and black .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The wheels were Improved Engine Green with red lining .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Cab roofs were white .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Goods engines were all - over olive green with black borders , similar to the pre-1870 colours .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: If fitted with Westinghouse brakes the black borders were edged with red lines .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Locomotives with names had the name applied in gold leaf to the tank side on tank locomotives , to a wheel splasher on tender locomotives .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The letters were edged with a thin red line and given depth with black shading .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This livery was one of the most ornate and distinctive used on British locomotives , and is remembered with nostalgia .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Carriages were all mahogany in colour , with white roofs and black chassis gear .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Initially the wood of the body was varnished , but as it became harder to maintain a high - quality varnish finish and it was painted in a similar - coloured paint .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Panel lining and other details were picked out with gold leaf .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: From 1905 to 1923 front - line express locomotives were a dark shade of umber .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Lining was black with a gilt line either side .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Cab roofs remained white .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Frames were black , wheels umber , and buffer beams returned to signal red .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The company 's initials were painted on the tender - or tank - sides ( initially ' L.B.& S.C.R. ' , but after 1911 the ampersand and the R were removed ) in gilt .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Secondary passenger locomotives had the same livery , but instead of gilt lining chrome yellow paint was used .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Goods engines were gloss black with double vermilion lining .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Names and numbers were in white letters with red shading .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Carriages were initially all olive green with white lining and detailing .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: From 1911 this changed to plain umber with black lettering picked out with gold shading .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Ferry services and ships

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR invested in cross-channel ferry services , initially from Shoreham to Dieppe .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Following the opening of the line to Newhaven in 1847 , it improved Newhaven harbour , building a wharf and dredging the channel .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A Newhaven – Dieppe service was established in 1847 , but discontinued soon afterwards .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1850 it established a Newhaven – Jersey ferry service , and in 1853 it reinstated the Dieppe service .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The London , Brighton and South Coast Railway ( New Lines ) Act 1862 ( 25 & 26 Vict. c. lxviii ) gave the LB&SCR power to own and operate its own steam vessels , so it instructed Chief Engineer Frederick Banister to greatly expand the port and its facilities .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1863 the Chemins de Fer de l'Ouest in France agreed to operate the Newhaven – Dieppe passenger service jointly , advertised as the " shortest and cheapest " route to Paris , but never the quickest because of the much longer time taken at sea than the rival Dover to Calais route .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: ( Newhaven harbour was taken over by the military authorities and the ferries requisitioned for the duration of the First World War . )

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1863 , the LB&SCR transferred the Jersey service to Littlehampton and soon afterwards established another between Littlehampton and Honfleur .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By 1880 lines connected the Ryde Pier and the Portsmouth Harbour ferry terminals .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was therefore a natural progression for the companies to acquire the ferry routes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: To do this the LB&SCR and the L&SWR formed the South Western and Brighton Railway Companies Steam Packet Service ( SW&BRCSPS ) , which bought the operators .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1884 the Isle of Wight Marine Transit Company started a goods rail ferry between the Hayling Island Branch Line at Langstone and the Bembridge branch line at St Helens quay .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The rail ferry PS Carrier , designed to carry railway trucks , was moved from Scotland .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The project was unsuccessful and , despite being acquired by the LB&SCR in 1886 , ended in 1888 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR operated a significant number of ships in its own right , jointly with Chemins de Fer de l'Ouest , and as a part of the SW&BRCSPS .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Structures , buildings and civil engineering The LB&SCR inherited significant structures , buildings and other civil engineering features , including :

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Bridges and viaducts – the Ouse Valley Viaduct , London Road viaduct , the Lewes Road viaduct Moulsecoomb .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Norwood Junction flyover , the world 's first railway overpass .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Tunnels – Merstham , Balcombe , Haywards Heath , Clayton and Patcham , Ditchling Road ( Brighton ) and Falmer Stations – Modular station buildings at Brighton , Croydon , Redhill and Reigate Road , Horley , Three Bridges and Hassocks , designed by David Mocatta .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR inherited or built 20 termini , the most significant at London Bridge , London Victoria , Brighton , Portsmouth Harbour and Eastbourne .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Stations at major junctions included Clapham Junction , East Croydon , Three Bridges , Horsham , and Lewes .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The use of Mocatta 's modular station designs was not perpetuated .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: During the 1850s and 1860s most stations were constructed according to one or two stock designs prepared by the Chief Engineers , Robert Jacomb - Hood ( 1822 – 1900 ) and Frederick Banister ( 1860 – 1895 ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Banister had a love of Italianate architecture , meaning that during the 1880s the LB&SCR produced elaborate decorated architecture for many country stations , notably on the Bluebell and Cuckoo Lines .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The architect was Banister 's son-in - law , Thomas Myres .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Workshops and motive power depots

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The L&BR established a repair workshop at Brighton in 1840 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Between 1852 and 1957 more than 1,200 steam locomotives and prototype diesel - electric and electric locomotives were constructed there , before closure in 1962 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It had small locomotive repair facilities at New Cross and Battersea Park Depots in London .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: By the first decade of the 20th century , Brighton works could no longer cope with the repair and building of both locomotives and rolling stock .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1911 the LB&SCR built a carriage and wagon works at Lancing , which operated until 1965 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: A marine engineering workshop was established in the mid-1870s at Newhaven .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: There were engine sheds at Battersea Park , Brighton , Bognor Regis , Coulsdon North , West Croydon , Eastbourne , Epsom , Fratton ( joint ) Horsham , Littlehampton , Midhurst , New Cross Gate , Newhaven Town , St Leonards West Marina , Three Bridges and Tunbridge Wells West .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The headquarters and main offices were at Brighton station from 1846 until 1892 , when they were transferred to the former Terminus Hotel at London Bridge .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR opened the Terminus Hotel at London Bridge and the Grosvenor Hotel at London Victoria in 1861 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The first of these was not successful due to its site on the south bank and was turned into offices for the railway in 1892 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: It was destroyed by bombing in 1941 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The Grosvenor Hotel was rebuilt and enlarged in 1901 .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR acquired the Terminus Hotel next to Brighton station in 1877 , and operated the London and Paris Hotel at Newhaven .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The LB&SCR as an investment The 1867 report by the railway found that there had been ' a reckless disregard for shareholders ' interests for many years . '.

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: As a result , the company policies were several times subjected to criticism in pamphlets published during the 1870s and 1880s .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: The matter was settled in 1890 when the economist and editor of the Financial Times , William Ramage Lawson , conducted a detailed analysis of the financial performance and prospects of the LB&SCR , comparing it with other British railways .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: He concluded that the Brighton Deferred stock ' combined the highest return on investment , with the best prospect of future appreciation and the smallest risk of retrogression . '

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Among the reasons given for this opinion were :

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Well established route and freedom from competition Varied and well distributed sources of traffic Moderate working expenses due to high quality construction of the original route and good maintenance .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Energetic and prudent management From 1870 the LB&SCR appears to have been a well - run , enterprising and profitable railway for its shareholders .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Industrial relations

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: For its time , the LB&SCR was regarded as a good employer .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1851 it created a benevolent fund for staff who had become incapacitated , and from 1854 operated a savings bank .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1867 there was a two - day strike involving the drivers and firemen over their working hours , resolved by negotiation .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: In 1872 a superannuation fund was established for higher grades of staff , extended to become a pension fund for all staff in 1899 under the London , Brighton and South Coast Railway ( Pensions ) Act 1899 ( 62 & 63 Vict. c. liv ) .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: Labour relations between the railway management , locomotive crews and Brighton works staff declined markedly in the period 1905 and 1910 leading to several strikes and sackings .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This was partly due to increased union militancy and to the intransigency of the Locomotive Superintendent Douglas Earle Marsh .

source.page_title: London, Brighton and South Coast Railway

text: This situation improved under Marsh 's successor .
